title: What to return
sub: Task, ValueTask and the dangerous async void
cards/0/body:
Task: no result, but you can wait for it.
Task<T>: returns a T.
ValueTask<T>: the same, but with no allocation when the result is often ready at once (say, from a cache). You may await it only once.
cards/1/title: async void is for event handlers only
cards/1/body:
You can't await an async void: the caller never learns when the method finished. And you can't catch its exception from outside: it goes to the synchronization context and usually crashes the app.

Use async void only where an event dictates the signature: button.Click += async (s, e) => …
cards/2/options/0: You can't await it, and a try around the call won't catch its exception
cards/2/explain: No task means nothing to wait on and nothing to carry the exception.
cards/3/q: Which line is a design mistake?
cards/3/explain: SaveAsync isn't an event handler. It should be async Task so callers can await it.
cards/4/options/0: When the result is often ready at once and the method is called very often
cards/4/options/2: When the method waits a long time on the network
cards/4/explain: You only save on the fast path with no waiting. If the method always waits, there is hardly any difference.
cards/5/q: What must you not do with a ValueTask? Select all that apply.
cards/5/options/1: Await it from two places at once
cards/5/explain: Need more? Call .AsTask() and work with a regular task.
cards/5/deep: A ValueTask can wrap a reusable IValueTaskSource. After the first await, what it holds may already belong to another operation. Hence the strict rules.
cards/6/pairs/2/1: No allocation if ready at once
cards/7/explain: async Task is a method with no result that callers can await.
